archetype.name: Rebuilding (run-first, pass-starved)
archetype.definition: A third straight bottom-tier season in which a sound offensive line and a sure-tackling front seven keep games close, but a passing game that can't move the ball and a leaky secondary leave the Titans without a way to win.

report.headline: A sound front and sure tackling can't hide the league's worst scoring offense.
report.take:
The Titans are 0-5 and have earned most of it. They score 11.6 points a game, last in the league, gain 246.8 yards a game, also last, and own the 31st-ranked net EPA. This is not a new hole. They won three games in each of the last two seasons and ranked 30th in offensive EPA both years, so 2026 is a continuation, not a collapse. What has changed is shape: Saleh's team leans hard on the run (pass rate over expected -8.2, 28th) and has an offensive line that does its job, then asks Cam Ward to finish drives he can't finish.

The passing game is the whole problem. Ward has thrown for 896 yards in five starts, about 179 a game, and the offense's pass EPA ranks 31st. It isn't a protection story. The line has allowed 10 sacks (9th fewest), ranks 10th in pressure rate, and has the league's lowest stuff rate. Ward has clean enough pockets and still can't produce. Week 5 against Houston was the low point: 3 points, -16.9 passing EPA, four sacks and 83 penalty yards. That one game accounts for more than half the season's negative passing EPA, so the baseline is less awful than the total suggests, but even the 'good' weeks against Philadelphia and Baltimore only got the passing game to roughly break even.

The numbers flatter the defense. Ranking 10th in points allowed sits badly with a defense that ranks 25th in EPA, 27th against the pass, 31st on deep balls and 26th in pressure rate. Four of the five opponents rank 14th or worse on offense today, and the Titans' games have been slow, low-total affairs. The real strengths are structural: the third-lowest missed-tackle rate and a run defense that rarely gives up explosive plays. That keeps the floor up, but this defense doesn't take the ball away (two takeaways, both in Week 2) and doesn't get home. Add special teams costing 4.56 EPA a game, 31st, and there is no hidden-yardage source to steal a win.

There is a bit of bad luck in the 0-5. The point differential projects about 1.7 wins, and three losses came by six points or fewer. That is not a Better Than Its Record case. It's a bad team that has also been slightly unlucky, and the injury list is now gutting the secondary: both starting safeties are hurt and two corners are down. Expect the close losses to keep coming, with a couple of wins scraped out against the softer games on the back half of the schedule.

strengths.title: Line that blocks and protects
strengths.body: The front has the league's lowest stuff rate, converts short yardage at an elite clip, and keeps sacks among the ten lowest totals. This is a repeatable, scheme-and-personnel strength, not script noise, since it has held through trailing game states. It is the reason Pollard and the run game stay viable even when the passing attack stalls.

strengths.title: Sure tackling limits explosive runs
strengths.body: Third in missed-tackle rate and 7th in explosive run rate allowed: the front seven keeps runs in front of it and rarely gives up the chunk play. Tackling discipline like this usually holds, and it is the main reason points allowed look better than the EPA does.

strengths.title: Tight ends get erased
strengths.body: Opposing TE1s have scored 6.4 PPR points a game under their norm, the best mark in the league. The underneath zones and linebacker coverage are sound. The holes are deeper and wider, against secondary receivers.

concerns.title: A passing game that can't score
concerns.body: Pass EPA ranks 31st despite good protection, so the problem is decision-making, accuracy and separation rather than the line. The Houston game showed the floor, and nothing in five weeks suggests a jump. It mirrors last year's 30th-ranked offense, which makes it a real flaw, not a slump.

concerns.title: Secondary leaks deep, now short-handed
concerns.body: The defense is 31st in deep-pass EPA, gets almost no pressure, and opposing WR2s and WR3s have posted the league's worst EPA per target against it. With Hooker out, Winston awaiting an MRI and Flott and Williams hurt at corner, the back end is likely to get worse before it gets better. Points allowed should drift up toward what the EPA says.

concerns.title: No hidden yardage anywhere
concerns.body: Special teams cost 4.56 EPA a game, the turnover margin is -1 a game, and the defense has two takeaways. Some takeaway regression toward normal should come, but the special-teams drain looks like a real unit problem, and it is costing nearly half a game's margin every week.

trend.note: Weeks 2 through 4 were competitive losses by four, five and six points with near-neutral passing, but Week 5's 26-3 home loss to Houston was the worst game of the season by every measure. The injuries that followed hit the secondary hardest.

nextGame.headline: Pollard's best matchup yet, but Ward's top targets meet lockdown coverage
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis is a mediocre team (26th in net EPA, -2.8 point differential), but it fits the Titans in awkward ways. The Colts have the league's worst run defense by EPA and have let lead backs score 5.8 PPR points a game over their norm, also last. That is exactly where Tennessee wants to play. The catch is the passing game: the Colts allow the 3rd-lowest EPA to WR1s and the lowest to WR2s, and Carnell Tate and Wan'Dale Robinson take 67 of Ward's targets between them. If the Titans fall behind and have to throw, the matchup turns against them fast. On the other side, the Colts run the ball better than anyone by EPA, while their passing game ranks 29th.

Availability tilts both ways. The Colts are thin at receiver, with Alec Pierce on IR and Ashton Dulin and Darius Slayton out, plus Will Mallory on IR at tight end. That blunts their ability to exploit a Titans secondary missing Amani Hooker and possibly Kevin Winston Jr. and Cor'Dale Flott. The Colts also lose edge rusher Arden Key to IR and linebacker Jaylon Carlies, which weakens an already soft front against the run.

keyMatchups.title: Pollard against the league's worst run defense
keyMatchups.body: The Titans' line has the lowest stuff rate in football, and Indianapolis ranks 32nd in rush EPA allowed while missing Key and Carlies. If Tennessee keeps the game within a score, this is where its offense lives. The risk is game script: in the Houston blowout the Titans ran for only 57 yards.

keyMatchups.title: Ward's top two vs stingy outside coverage
keyMatchups.body: Tate leads the team with 37 targets and Robinson is next with 30, and the Colts have been among the stingiest teams in the league against opposing WR1s and WR2s. Expect Ward to need Spears, Pollard and Helm underneath, which caps the ceiling of an offense already struggling to score.

keyMatchups.title: Colts' ground game vs a tackling front
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis's offense is all run game: 1st in rush EPA, 29th in pass EPA, with its receiver room depleted. The Titans' run defense is only middling by EPA but rarely misses tackles. Whether it can force the Colts into obvious passing downs decides whether the battered secondary gets exposed.

nextGame.watch: Whether Tennessee is still handing off to Pollard into the second half. A close game keeps the run game alive. Trailing early pushes the Titans into throwing at Indianapolis's strength.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense's points-allowed ranking should slide, because the schedule gets much harder on offense (Cincinnati, Jacksonville twice, Dallas and Detroit all rank top-nine offensively) and the secondary is banged up. The takeaway drought should ease somewhat, and the special-teams drain may too. The passing offense is the anchor, though, and two years of 30th-plus rankings say not to expect a leap. The run game and protection keep enough games close to steal a few.

The realistic win spots are Cleveland at home, Washington at home, the Colts rematch in Week 15, and the season finale at Houston. Dallas and Detroit field bottom-two defenses that could let even this offense put up points, but both also outscore people. Expect two to four wins, with the Titans losing most weeks by roughly a score.
swingFactors: Whether Ward's passing climbs from the Week 5 floor back toward break-even
How long Hooker, Winston and Flott are out

bets.reason: Four of the Titans' five games went under, averaging about 33 combined points, and this is the highest total they've faced. Both teams lean on the run, and the Colts' passing game ranks 29th in EPA and is missing Pierce, Dulin, Slayton and Mallory. The Colts' own games have run higher, which keeps this a modest edge.

Indianapolis is last in rush EPA allowed and last against lead backs, and it is missing Key and Carlies. Tennessee's line has the league's lowest stuff rate, and the Titans stay run-heavy (pass rate over expected -8.2). The risk is an early deficit like Week 5.

confidence.note: Five-game sample, but it fits a two-year pattern; secondary injuries add uncertainty.
